title: 'Links with the British royal family would eventually prove crucial': How DNA solved the 70-year mystery of what happened to the executed members of the last Russian imperial family
summary: In this excerpt from "The Secrets of our DNA," geneticist Turi King examines how DNA was used to reveal the ultimate fate of the last members of the House of Romanov.
body: In 1917, the Russian Revolution was in full swing. Tsar Nicholas II had abdicated, and he and his family were exiled to a remote Siberian town. There were plans to get the family to the U.K., but King George V (Nicholas' first cousin) and the British government withdrew their offer of asylum over concerns of the ramifications. After the Russian Provisional Government was overthrown by the more extreme Bolsheviks in October 1917, Nicholas, his wife, their children and several members of the family's staff were moved to Ipatiev House in Yekaterinburg, where, in July 1918, they were executed. Their bodies were hidden and remained lost to time ‪for nearly a century —‬ until modern technology, with some help from the British royal family, unraveled the fascinating story of their disappearance. In this excerpt from " The Secrets of Our DNA: How Genetics Has Changed the World " (Pegasus Books, 2026), author Turi King , director of the Center for Evolution at the University of Bath, looks back at the incredible story of how DNA was used to solve a major mystery of modern history: What happened to the last members of the House of Romanov? title: A widely used antibiotic for acne and infections is linked to risk of pregnancy loss, new study finds
summary: A common antibiotic may be linked to a higher risk of miscarriage and stillbirth when used early in pregnancy, a new study suggests.
body: Taking doxycycline, a commonly prescribed antibiotic, during the first trimester of pregnancy may increase the risk of pregnancy loss, a new study suggests. The antibiotic is broad-spectrum, meaning it targets a wide range of bacteria. It's often used to treat acne, respiratory infections and sexually transmitted infections, such as chlamydia and syphilis. Doctors generally avoid prescribing the drug during the second and third trimesters because it belongs to a class of antibiotics that can bind to calcium in developing bones. Animal studies suggest that this may disrupt fetal bone development. However, evidence on doxycycline's safety during early pregnancy has been mixed and limited. The new study, published Tuesday (Nov. 10) in the journal Annals of Internal Medicine , provides clearer evidence of a link between doxycycline use in the first trimester and pregnancy loss. "I would advise physicians to carefully consider the benefit-risk balance when prescribing doxycycline to women who are pregnant or planning a pregnancy," study first author Almut Winterstein , a pharmacist and drug-safety researcher at the University of Florida, told Live Science in an email. title: When a battery dies, you replace it — how jumpstarting cells with fresh mitochondria could revolutionize medicine
summary: Mitochondria can become compromised in a number of medical conditions. What if they could be replaced like batteries?
body: A newborn baby's heart is roughly the size of a walnut — which makes open-heart surgery challenging. Each year, about 10,000 babies in the United States are born with critical heart defects that may require surgery to fix, often fairly soon after birth. In these infants, the two major arteries of the heart could have swapped positions or the left side of the heart may be far too small to pump properly . Even if their surgeries go well, these babies face perilous recoveries. A complication can arise when blood flows back into the repaired heart, triggering what's known as an ischemia-reperfusion injury. This can stun the organ, triggering extensive damage that requires doctors to place the baby on a life-support machine that pumps and infuses oxygen into blood to sub in for the hampered heart and lungs. Only about 40% of newborns make it off the machine, because often, their tiny hearts don't recover. Doctors and scientists at Boston Children's Hospital have been working to improve those odds using a creative idea: replacing the fuel source in damaged heart cells to help them bounce back from injury. That fuel source is mitochondria, the "batteries" found in most cells in the body.…

title: More people could count as obese under newly proposed definition — here's what you need to know
summary: A new study supports a more nuanced approach to obesity diagnosis. Here's what to know.
body: Obesity is linked to a range of health problems ‪—‬ including heart disease, diabetes and early death ‪—‬ but it can be hard to know who is most at risk for these outcomes. Doctors and researchers often use body mass index ( BMI ) as a convenient tool to assess patients, but this metric does not account for individual differences in body composition, scientists have long argued . "BMI misses a lot of information," Dr. Francesco Rubino , a professor of bariatric and metabolic surgery at King's College London, told Live Science. Rubino recently chaired a team of 56 experts that was assembled to better define obesity and develop new diagnostic criteria for the condition. First proposed in January 2025, their new framework includes more body measurements beyond BMI and distinguishes between "preclinical" and "clinical" obesity. Now, a new study published Wednesday (Nov. 11) in the journal Nature confirms that these new criteria could detect obesity with greater precision than BMI alone. In other words, with the new approach, more people would be accurately diagnosed with obesity and fewer people would be misdiagnosed than are with BMI alone. title: A man swallowed a bone, and‬ 15 years later, doctors found it in his appendix
summary: A man's appendix had to be removed, but not for dangerous inflammation, as you might expect.
body: The patient: A 45-year-old man in Italy The symptoms: The man went to the emergency room because he had a sharp pain in his lower-right abdomen. What happened next: When doctors examined the man, the type of pain and the location of his discomfort suggested that he might have appendicitis , or inflammation of the appendix. Appendicitis can be dangerous because it can cause the appendix to burst and release bacteria from the bowels into the abdominal cavity, thereby infecting the cavity's lining. This infection, called peritonitis , can spread to the bloodstream and cause the life-threatening condition sepsis , which kicks the immune system into overdrive. Even though the patient had acute pain in his lower-right abdomen, he did not show signs of peritonitis , such as fever, nausea, symptoms of dehydration and an elevated heart rate, according to a report of his case . His doctors then performed abdominal ultrasound scans and found that the man's abdominal organs, including the appendix, appeared normal, with no signs of inflammation. title: Women often get cold more easily than men — a mouse study offers hints why
summary: A new study points to testosterone and proteins in the skin as reasons why males and females experience temperatures differently.
body: It's a common observation that women often prefer warmer temperatures and feel cold more easily than men do, and the same trend appears among females of other species. Now, a study offers new clues as to what drives this preference — and testosterone may play a part. Skin carries sensors to detect heat and cold that influence each organism's decision to stay in or move out of an environment. The new study, published Oct. 28 in the Journal of Physiology , found that these sensors activate at higher temperatures in female mice, which appears to shift their preferred temperature roughly 7 degrees Fahrenheit (4 degrees Celsius) higher than that of male mice. Testosterone seems to influence this difference in activation. "You could say it's just a cute observation of no particular importance," said study co-author Peter McNaughton , a pharmacologist at King's College London who studies pain, thermal sensation and thermoregulation. "[But] it's got practical ramifications," in that it might be important in designing buildings and spaces that accommodate people, he told Live Science. title: I almost died from flu. My life didn't go back to normal after.
summary: Madi Allen was 12 years old when she almost died from flu. Now 28, she shared her story with Live Science.
body: In February 2011, Madi Allen, a healthy 12-year-old in Central Illinois, who loved playing sports, almost died from the flu. The influenza B virus resulted in her developing necrotizing pneumonia, where the infection triggers inflammation that destroys the tissue of the lungs, methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), and her kidneys shut down. She was put on life support and dialysis, and was intubated for five weeks. She spent another two months in hospital and a decade recovering from the damage caused. Allen, now 28, shared her experience with Live Science. I was 12 years old when it all started. I was just a normal seventh grader, I played soccer and basketball. I didn't really have any health issues beforehand — just sports-induced asthma. That weekend, I started to feel a little sick, but nothing too bad. My mom kept giving me over-the-counter medicine and it would work for a bit, then once it wore off, it would get really bad. I'd planned to go to one of my friend's birthday parties then spend the night with my best friend. title: 'Life is too brief to leave this planet': Live Science readers share whether they'd go to Mars, despite health risks
summary: Live Science readers respond to a recent poll about whether they'd visit the Red Planet even with potential health risks.
body: For centuries, Mars has been seen as a potential place for future human settlements. But long-duration space travel comes with serious risks to astronauts' health , including those resulting from cosmic radiation and the effects of microgravity . A new study found that rats that were exposed to radiation similar to what astronauts might encounter during a Mars mission developed more scar tissue around their hearts' small blood vessels compared with a control group. Although the findings haven't been validated in humans, the results contribute to growing concerns about the potential effects of long-haul space missions on astronauts' health. Given these new findings, Live Science asked its readers whether they'd travel to the Red Planet , despite these potential health risks. Over 240 readers weighed in, with 65% picking "No, I don't think the risks are worth it." Interestingly enough, the comments reflect a slightly different trend. One reader wrote, "Any pioneers who travel to Mars will be facing the prospect of death and never coming back. Even if they make it back, there are any number of health issues that could come up. title: 50% of long COVID patients show improvement in 3 years — but the condition tends to linger in those with this subtype
summary: About half of people with long COVID see meaningful improvement in their symptoms after three years, a new study found.
body: Symptoms of long COVID ease in half of patients within three years of the infection that kicked off their illness. That's the primary conclusion of a new study that tracked over 1,000 patients with long COVID, a chronic condition that can emerge after an infection with the SARS-CoV-2 virus. Among the patients, the chance of improvement varied sharply depending on how the condition affected their bodily systems. In the study, published Tuesday (Nov. 3) in the journal Annals of Internal Medicine , roughly 60% of patients whose predominant symptoms were changes to their ability to taste or smell had significantly improved three years after their first positive test. But less than 20% of those with a multisystem presentation had improved in that time frame. This latter group had symptoms that affected their cardiac, nervous and gastrointestinal systems, among others. An expert told Live Science that the condition resembled myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS), which often arises after an infection and similarly impacts a wide range of bodily systems.
